# Shell guard friction

<!-- Generated by scripts/measure-shell-friction.ts. Edit the corpus, the field file or the script, not this page. -->

The shell guard refused **19 of 101** routine commands in the corpus: commands that read, or that write nothing the contract governs. It refused 10 of 15 commands that write a governed source file from the shell, and 4 of 4 that change the contract or the protection. Refusing those two groups is what the guard is for.

## Method

1. Build a scratch TypeScript project with a Makefile, shell, Node, Bun and Python scripts, two commits and a second branch. Approve a contract for it in enforce mode.
2. Send each corpus command to the real pre hook (`pregate hook pre --harness claude-code`) as a Claude Code `Bash` call. The hook judges the command. The command is never run.
3. Record the decision and, for a denial, its cause.

The corpus is [`shell-friction-corpus.json`](shell-friction-corpus.json): hand-assembled commands for git, npm, Bun, make, Python, plain shell and Pregate itself. It is not a sample of what agents run, so the counts below are not a rate for any real session. The engine ran from source.

The result depends on the machine. This run: darwin arm64. The guard resolves a bare command name on `PATH` and reads the file when it is a script. On this machine these corpus commands are scripts: `cd`, `command`, `npm`, `npx`, `pregate`, `type`, `wait`.

## Corpus result

| What the command does | Commands | Refused |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Reads only | 51 | 8 |
| Writes nothing the contract governs | 50 | 11 |
| Writes a governed source file from the shell | 15 | 10 |
| Changes the contract or the protection | 4 | 4 |

### Source and contract writes the guard let through

| rm-source | `rm src/a.ts` |

## Field sample

One Claude Code session developed this repository for several days on macOS, with the hooks of the installed engine (0.0.3) registered. Project consent was not active for the whole session, and while it is inactive only `protected-path` and `hook-switch` can refuse, so the sample understates an enabled project. The guard refused **16 of 911** shell commands (9 `hook-switch`, 3 `protected-path`, 3 `shell-write`, 1 `shell-admin`). The commands are not published. Each refusal was read and labeled:

| Refusals | Verdict | Cause | Shape |
| ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| 6 | false positive | `hook-switch` | `bun scripts/<generator>.ts`: a repository script that prints documentation. Its text names control commands, so the scan of a literal script reads it as one that runs them. |
| 5 | intended | `hook-switch, shell-admin, protected-path` | An unattended approval, a second copy of the engine run with another `HOME`, a compiled engine binary named as an argument, a heredoc that writes a project file, and `rm -rf` of a contract folder. |
| 3 | by design, no harm intended | `shell-write` | A script or a write target named through a variable (`bun $S/tool.ts`, `cd $S/dir && echo … > file`). The guarantees page documents this refusal. All three touched a scratch folder outside the project. |
| 2 | unclear | `protected-path` | A read-only script that received the lock file of another project as an argument. |

One session on one repository is a sample, not a rate.

## Keep, trim, hold

No anti-evasion rule is added until the held refusals below are settled. The guard still refuses routine work that it should not.

**Keep.** Every refusal of a command that changes the contract or the protection. The refusal of a shell write to a governed source file, and of a script or a target named through a variable: both are documented in [Guarantees and limits](../guarantees.md), and the edit tool is the supported route.

**Trimmed.** The first measurement refused 32 of 101 routine commands. Three causes protected nothing, because the refused reading of the command is not what the shell runs. They are fixed, and the numbers above are from after the fix:

- A shell builtin (`cd`, `type`, `wait`, `read`, `umask`) was looked up on `PATH`. macOS ships `/usr/bin/cd` and its siblings as scripts with a computed command name, so the guard read `cd src` as an unnamed command. The shell runs its builtin and never that file.
- `bun test` was read as Bun running a script named `test`. With a `test` directory in the project, that path is not a readable file and the command was refused. `test` is a Bun subcommand.
- `pregate layers` and `pregate compile` were refused in an enabled project. They read, or they prepare a review that only a human approves, like `pregate rules add`. The skill tells the agent to run them.

**Hold, for a maintainer decision.** Each of these has a real bypass behind it, so trimming is a trade:

- An installed tool that is a script, such as `npm` and `npx`, is scanned like a project script and refused because it uses the file system. A native tool with the same behavior (`bun`, `pnpm`) is not scanned. One option: scan a script found outside every enabled root for control commands only.
- A literal read-only script is refused when it imports a file-system module (`node scripts/report.mjs`, `python3 scripts/count.py`). The scan cannot tell a read from a write.
- A script whose text names a control command in prose or in generated documentation is refused as if it ran it. This is the false positive of the field sample.
